title: Homer's Iliad Found Inside a 1,600-Year-Old Egyptian Mummy — a First in Archaeology
summary: In a stunning convergence of literature and burial ritual, archaeologists have uncovered a 1,600-year-old mummy with a papyrus of Homer's Iliad placed on its abdomen. The find, from the Al Bahnasa necropolis at ancient Oxyrhynchus, marks the first time a Greek literary text — rather than a magical or ritual one — has been found intentionally incorporated into mummification. The discovery was made by the Oxyrhynchus Archaeological Mission, led by Maite Mascort and Esther Pons from the University of Barcelona. During excavations in late 2025, a team directed by Núria Castellano unearthed a Roman-era mummy in Tomb 65 of Sector 22. Resting on the body was a papyrus that conservators and papyrologists later identified as a passage from the "Catalogue of Ships" in Book II of the Iliad. This section famously lists the Greek forces that sailed to Troy. Professor Ignasi-Xavier Adiego, the project's director, explained that while Greek papyri have been found in funerary contexts before, they were always magical spells. "The real novelty is finding a literary papyrus in a funerary context," he said. Oxyrhynchus, located about 190 kilometers south of Cairo, is renowned for its vast trove of preserved papyri, but this is unprecedented. The mummy was part of a complex of three limestone burial chambers containing Roman-era remains and decorated wooden sarcophagi, though many had been damaged by looters. The discovery raises intriguing questions: Why was the Iliad chosen? Was it a personal favorite of the deceased, or did the epic hold symbolic meaning for the afterlife? The team presented their findings at a lecture series at the University of Barcelona, and further analysis may shed light on this ancient literary mystery.
why_it_matters: This find rewrites our understanding of how ancient Egyptians and Greeks blended their cultures in death. It suggests that literature held a power beyond entertainment – perhaps even a passport to the afterlife – connecting modern readers to the idea that stories can accompany us beyond the final breath.

background_read: The Iliad, traditionally credited to the poet Homer, was composed around the 8th century BCE and remains one of the most influential works of Western literature. Oxyrhynchus (modern Al Bahnasa, about 190 km south of Cairo) became famous after 1896, when British archaeologists Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt found a vast rubbish mound there, yielding thousands of papyrus fragments – including lost works by Sophocles, Aristotle, and early Christian gospels. Usually, funerary papyri from Egypt contain magical spells or copies of the Book of the Dead to guide the soul. Finding a purely literary Greek text placed on a mummy’s abdomen is a genuine puzzle. The ‘Catalogue of Ships’ passage is a long, rhythmic list of the Greek commanders and the number of ships they brought to the Trojan War, a roll‑call of heroes that might have held symbolic power or personal significance for the deceased. The tomb, though looted, still held decorated wooden sarcophagi, showing the burial was of high status. This discovery blurs the line between Greek literary culture and Egyptian burial traditions in Roman‑ruled Egypt.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A 1,600‑year‑old mummy with an unexpected treasure – a papyrus of Homer’s Iliad – challenges what scholars thought about funerary texts.
DISCOVERY CONTEXT: Found in Tomb 65, Sector 22 of the Al Bahnasa necropolis (ancient Oxyrhynchus) by a Spanish‑led mission.
└─ TEAM: Maite Mascort and Esther Pons directed the 2025 excavation.
THE ARTIFACT: A papyrus lying on the mummy’s abdomen, identified as the ‘Catalogue of Ships’ from Book II of the Iliad.
└─ DETAIL: Passage lists the Greek forces that sailed to Troy.
NOVELTY QUOTED: Ignasi‑Xavier Adiego says, ‘The real novelty is finding a literary papyrus in a funerary context’ – earlier magical spells were the norm.
SITE SIGNIFICANCE: Oxyrhynchus is famous for thousands of papyri, but never before a literary text in a burial.
ARCHAEOLOGICAL SETTING: Three limestone chambers with Roman‑era remains and decorated wooden sarcophagi, though damaged by looters.
OPEN QUESTIONS: Why the Iliad? A personal favourite, or symbolic meaning for the afterlife? Further analysis may tell.

perspectives.description: Classicists and archaeologists are elated because a Greek epic placed deliberately on a mummy hints at a personal, emotional tie to literature. It raises the possibility that other burials might contain similarly overlooked ‘bookish’ objects, sparking a re‑examination of museum collections and future digs.

Sceptics note that the tomb had been looted, so the papyrus’s original position and context might be compromised. It is also possible the text was simply reused scrap, not a meaningful choice. Without the full burial record, any symbolic interpretation remains speculative.

Roman Egypt was a melting pot where Greek was the language of administration and prestige, while Egyptian religion dominated burial customs. This discovery illustrates a historical pattern of cultural syncretism: a Greek text on an Egyptian‑style mummy reflects how identities merged under imperial rule, with literature perhaps serving as a status marker even in death.

Multispectral imaging and DNA analysis of the mummy could reveal its age, health, and maybe even its profession – clues to why the Iliad was chosen. If similar papyri are found in other necropolises, scholars may need to reassess the role of literature in funerary rituals across the ancient Mediterranean. The mission’s future lecture series and publications may inspire a dedicated search for more ‘book‑mummies’.
